hero.intro: Camera trapping, herpetology, and a decade of fieldwork across remote landscapes — from the Sierra Nevada to New Zealand's Te Araroa.

statement.label: Artist statement
statement.pull: The camera trap is a form of deep listening — a way of attending to a place long after you've left it.
paragraphs: I spend months in landscapes that most people never see, building trust with the terrain. The work is slow, methodical, and often humbling. You set a trap, return weeks later, and find the forest has been carrying on perfectly well without your witness.

My practice sits at the edge of natural history and fine art photography — rooted in fieldcraft, shaped by a naturalist's curiosity, and driven by a belief that careful attention to the wild world is one of the most urgent things a photographer can do.

about.headline:
Yielding to the pull
toward the edge
of things
paragraphs: I grew up chasing snakes through vacant lots and spent my early twenties making my way across New Zealand's Te Araroa trail — 3,000 kilometres, mostly alone. That journey rewired something. I came back with a camera trap and a notebook and haven't stopped since.

My fieldwork has taken me through the Cascades and Sierra Nevada, deep into Central American cloud forest, and across some of the most remote terrain in the South Pacific. I document the animals that don't wait to be photographed.
I'm available for editorial assignments, brand partnerships, and conservation projects that require both photographic skill and genuine naturalist knowledge.

quote.text: The places that matter most are the ones that ask something of you.
